summary: This informational document describes privacy issues of using the DNS and gives general observations about typical current privacy practices. It is an analysis of the present situation and does not prescribe solutions. It obsoletes RFC 7626.

plainLanguage.summary: Asking the DNS for a website name can reveal where you are going. This document explains who can see those questions and what privacy troubles that causes.

questions: who can see my dns queries
subtitle: Where a DNS lookup leaks information about you, from your device to the root servers.

tldr.problem: Almost every activity on the Internet starts with a DNS query, and those queries reveal who asked about what to many parties along the path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyses privacy risks in the DNS data, on the wire for unencrypted and encrypted transports, and in recursive resolvers and authoritative name servers. It describes the present situation and sets no requirements.
tldr.outcome: It gives a shared picture of the risks that other work can build on. It obsoletes RFC 7626.

today: RFC 9076 is an Informational RFC published in July 2021 that obsoletes RFC 7626, and no later RFC obsoletes it. It analyses the situation as it stood at the time of writing and sets no requirements.

sections.title: How a DNS Lookup Exposes Information
sections.content:
A client, the stub resolver, sends a query to a recursive resolver. With a cold cache, the resolver asks the root name servers, then the .com name servers, then the example.com name servers. All of these are authoritative name servers. The key privacy point is that each of them receives the original full question, not a derived one, unless the resolver does QNAME minimization as described in RFC 7816.

Because the stub resolver typically has no cache, the recursive resolver sees all of the DNS traffic, while authoritative servers see only what the cache misses. Almost all DNS traffic is currently sent unencrypted, and almost all queries use UDP, although DNS over TLS (RFC 7858) and DNS over HTTPS (RFC 8484) are increasingly deployed.

The RFC also separates three kinds of request behind a web page view: the primary request for the name the user chose, secondary requests for embedded content that the browser makes without the user's knowledge, and tertiary requests made by the DNS service itself.
sections.plainLanguage: When you look up a name, your question gets passed along, and each helper sees the whole question, not just their little part.

sections.title: Scope of the Analysis
sections.content:
The document focuses on privacy risks for the end user, the one performing DNS requests. It considers both pervasive surveillance and more focused surveillance. It does not compare the protections of individual networks and makes only general observations about typical current practices.

Out of scope are privacy risks for the holder of a zone, privacy risks for recursive operators such as leakage of private namespaces or blocklists, non-privacy risks such as cache poisoning, and privacy risks of other protocols that use DNS information. The RFC also notes that a user may have many devices on many networks, so a full per-user analysis is not attempted.
sections.plainLanguage: This document looks at what could happen to the person asking questions. It leaves other worries, like fake answers, for other documents.

sections.title: Privacy Risks in the DNS Data
sections.content:
DNS data is public in the sense that public authoritative servers answer ordinary queries without authenticating the client. A single transaction is different, because it reveals both who asked and what was asked. A sequence of transactions can also be linked to show individual use patterns.

Two fields matter most in a request: the QNAME and the source IP address. The QNAME shows what the user does. A query for the MX records of a small domain, for example, suggests a communication relationship, and some QNAMEs embed the software in use. Between a stub and its resolver, the source address is the user's machine. Towards authoritative servers it is usually the resolver's address, but the EDNS client subnet option (RFC 7871) can pass client address information along.

The RFC also notes that no standardized client identifiers exist in the DNS payload, that DNS Cookies are not designed to track users, and that resolver cache contents can be probed to learn about clients (cache snooping).
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone may look in the phone book, but a list of which names you looked up says a lot about you.

sections.title: Risks on the Wire
sections.content:
Unencrypted DNS can be read by an eavesdropper like any other traffic, and DNSSEC explicitly excludes confidentiality from its goals. Even if the later HTTPS connection is encrypted, the lookup before it is not. The best place to tap is between the stub and the recursive resolver, because caching does not thin the traffic there. The attack surface grows with where the resolver is: on the device, at the local network edge, in the access provider's network, or at a public DNS service.

Encrypted transports directly mitigate passive surveillance of the payload, but residual risks remain. Fingerprints such as the IPv4 TTL, IPv6 Hop Limit or TCP window size can identify client operating systems. Default settings such as TLS version, cipher suite choice or session resumption could fingerprint an application, and traffic analysis of unpadded encrypted traffic can correlate message sizes and timing with upstream unencrypted queries.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing your question on a postcard lets every mail carrier read it. A sealed envelope hides the words, but people can still guess from its size and timing.

sections.title: Risks in the Servers
sections.content:
In the language of RFC 6973, DNS servers are enablers, and they become observers when they collect data. Query logs may be kept for a long time, shared with researchers, or passed to outside observers. Recursive resolvers see all of a client's traffic, so the choice of resolver has direct privacy consequences. Most users never change their defaults, so they implicitly accept the network's resolver, whose privacy policy may vary or be unavailable. Some networks and users choose a large public resolver, which typically publishes a privacy policy but concentrates traffic with a few operators.

The RFC also covers active attacks, where an attacker can impersonate an encrypted resolver unless the client was configured securely with the server identity. It covers blocking of access to resolvers offering encrypted transport, and the extra identifiers DoH can carry through HTTP. Authoritative servers see less because of caching and QNAME minimization, but a local resolver can reveal the end client's address to them, and ECS can remove the shielding of a large shared resolver.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper who passes your question along hears every question you ask, so it matters a lot which helper you pick.

sections.title: Inference, Attacks and Legal Questions
sections.content:
Observers can draw inferences from DNS data. A study cited in the RFC found that users could be re-identified from their pattern of DNS queries, with 73.1% of day-to-day links correctly established. Even malware-detection research on DNS traffic is described as technically a privacy attack, since it shows how much DNS traffic reveals.

The RFC points to the Snowden documents as evidence that DNS is used in mass surveillance, naming the MORECOWBELL and QUANTUMTHEORY programs. On legal matters it says that, to the authors' knowledge, there are no specific privacy laws for DNS data in any country, and that applying general privacy laws is not easy and has no known court precedent.

The Security Considerations section notes that the document is entirely about privacy. It lays out the problem without setting requirements or defining solutions, and points to documents such as RFC 8932 for recommendations to DNS privacy operators.
sections.plainLanguage: Even without your name, someone watching your questions over time can often tell it is you, like recognizing a friend by how they walk.
